paragraphs: Maximum inner product search finds vectors that score highly against a query under an inner product. This operation appears in prediction for low-rank matrix factorization and deep learning models. The paper focuses on a practical requirement: performing the search within a computational budget while retaining useful results.

The authors develop Greedy-MIPS by examining the structure of the search problem. Its design explicitly accommodates a budget, making the trade-off between computation and search quality part of the method. This matters because a fast search procedure is more useful when its computational effort can be adjusted to the resources available.

The reported experiments show strong performance relative to existing approaches. In one example with half a million candidate vectors, each with 200 dimensions, Greedy-MIPS is 200 times faster than naive search while achieving top-five precision above 75%. This illustrates a substantial speed–quality trade-off in that example; it does not establish the same speedup or precision for every collection of vectors.
neurips-2017-a-greedy-approach-for-budge.tldr: Greedy-MIPS makes maximum inner product search adjustable to a computational budget, with strong reported speed–quality trade-offs.

paragraphs: Neural networks use nonlinear response functions to transform their inputs. This paper studies these functions in stochastic networks, where hidden units are random variables. Its goal is to place several familiar nonlinearities inside a shared probabilistic framework so that the response functions themselves can participate in learning.

The construction uses Gaussian distributions restricted by two truncation boundaries. Adjusting those boundaries allows the framework to generate different nonlinearities, including sigmoid, tanh, and ReLU. These choices are therefore connected through the parameters of one probabilistic construction. The framework integrates with existing stochastic networks and allows their nonlinearities to be learned alongside their weights.

The authors evaluate the approach within restricted Boltzmann machines, temporal restricted Boltzmann machines, and truncated Gaussian graphical models. They report performance improvements across these integrations. The contribution combines a common mathematical description of widely used nonlinearities with a way to adapt them during training, and the experiments support the usefulness of that flexibility in the stochastic models examined.
neurips-2017-a-probabilistic-framework-f.tldr: A framework built from truncated Gaussian distributions lets stochastic neural networks learn their nonlinearities together with their weights.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover a partition of observed samples into groups using a flexible probabilistic model. Its target is exact clustering: identifying the partition itself with high probability. This gives the analysis a concrete statistical objective, beyond simply producing groups that look compact under an optimization criterion.

The proposed estimator uses convex semidefinite optimization and can be understood as a corrected relaxation of K-means. The authors analyze it with finite-sample guarantees, rather than relying only on what happens as the dataset grows indefinitely. Within their model and analysis, the estimator achieves optimal or nearly optimal performance for recovering the partition.

A central result is adaptivity to both the effective dimension of the problem and the unknown number of groups. This connects the recovery guarantees to the problem's underlying complexity while accommodating uncertainty about how many clusters exist. Numerical experiments on simulated high-dimensional data compare the method with classical clustering algorithms and illustrate its performance alongside the theoretical analysis.
neurips-2017-adaptive-clustering-through.tldr: A convex relaxation of K-means provides strong partition-recovery guarantees that adapt to effective dimension and an unknown number of clusters.

paragraphs: Image restoration uses information about plausible images to help reconstruct a clean image from degraded observations. This paper introduces a prior that directly represents a Gaussian-smoothed natural image distribution. It places that prior within a Bayesian estimation formulation, which also supports restoration when the noise is not known in advance.

The key connection is between the gradient of the prior and a mean-shift vector on the natural image distribution. This provides a direction for updating an image using the prior's distributional information. The authors learn the resulting vector field with denoising autoencoders, connecting a learned restoration component to an explicit statistical objective.

The learned field is used in gradient descent to minimize Bayes risk. The authors demonstrate competitive results for noise-blind deblurring, super-resolution, and demosaicing. Together, these applications show how the same prior-based construction can support several restoration problems. The stated finding is competitive performance across these tasks, supported by a mathematical link between the image prior and the learned update directions.
neurips-2017-deep-mean-shift-priors-for-.tldr: The paper connects a smoothed natural image prior to mean-shift updates learned by denoising autoencoders for Bayesian image restoration.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to distribute learning across processors as datasets grow and applications demand more accurate, confident predictions. It proposes a general parallelisation scheme that applies to a broad class of learning algorithms without requiring new mathematical derivations or dedicated implementation work for each algorithm, while preserving theoretical performance guarantees.

For many algorithms, the scheme reduces runtime to polylogarithmic time using quasi-polynomially many processing units. This is a theoretical statement about how computation scales when substantial parallel resources are available. The authors position it as progress toward efficient parallel learning in the sense of Nick's Class, rather than claiming a complete resolution of that question.

The speed improvement comes with a stated statistical cost: larger sample complexity. Parallel computation therefore trades additional data requirements for reduced runtime. An empirical study with fixed processor counts and fixed numbers of examples supports the scheme's potential in realistic settings. The contribution combines broad applicability with an explicit account of the resources needed to obtain its theoretical speed gains.
neurips-2017-effective-parallelisation-f.tldr: A broadly applicable parallelisation scheme reduces learning time while preserving guarantees, at the cost of needing more samples.

paragraphs: Online kernel learning offers a rich space of prediction functions, but processing each new observation becomes expensive as the history grows. Second-order methods can achieve logarithmic regret, meaning their accumulated loss approaches the comparator's loss relatively quickly. Their usual quadratic per-step cost, however, makes that statistical advantage computationally demanding.

The proposed method, PROS-N-KONS, uses Nyström sketching to project inputs into a smaller space and performs second-order updates there. Crucially, the embedding changes over time to preserve accuracy. This addresses a weakness of fixed-size approximations: an adversary can exploit the restriction when the approximation space or number of retained support vectors stops growing.

The analysis gives logarithmic regret while making per-step computation depend on the problem's effective dimension rather than directly on the elapsed number of observations. This ties computational demands to the structure of the learning problem. Experiments on large-scale benchmarks show favorable performance, supporting the combination of adaptive approximation and second-order optimization as a way to manage both prediction quality and computational cost.
neurips-2017-efficient-second-order-onli.tldr: PROS-N-KONS combines an adaptive kernel embedding with second-order updates to achieve logarithmic regret at a cost governed by effective dimension.

paragraphs: Count-based exploration encourages a reinforcement learning agent to visit unfamiliar states. It works well in small discrete settings, but counting exact states becomes problematic in high-dimensional or continuous environments, where observations may rarely repeat. This paper investigates whether a simple generalization can retain the approach's practical value in deep reinforcement learning.

The method maps states to hash codes and counts those codes in a hash table. It then computes an exploration reward bonus from the counts using the classic count-based approach. Sharing a code lets observations contribute to the same count. The authors find that even simple hash functions can produce strong results, with learned, domain-dependent codes potentially improving performance further.

Their analysis identifies two important properties of a useful hash function: appropriate granularity and preservation of information relevant to the task. Experiments achieve near state-of-the-art performance on continuous control tasks and Atari games. These findings support hashing as a simple, effective exploration baseline; they do not transfer the small-state theoretical guarantees automatically to every high-dimensional setting.
neurips-2017-exploration-a-study-of-coun.tldr: Counting hashed states provides a simple exploration strategy with strong empirical results in high-dimensional and continuous reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation estimates the long-term reward associated with following a policy. Gradient-based temporal difference methods use linear function approximation to make this possible in large or continuous state spaces. The paper asks how accurately these methods can learn from a finite amount of data, given that collecting experience consumes time and reward.

Earlier finite-sample analysis assumed independent observations. The authors instead analyze data generated by a Markov process, capturing the dependence between successive experiences in reinforcement learning. They derive bounds for general convex-concave saddle point problems and then apply those bounds to gradient-based temporal difference policy evaluation.

The results establish convergence with variants of the step size and show how the convergence rate depends on that choice. The Markov process's mixing time enters as a coefficient: faster mixing yields faster convergence in the bounds. This also provides an explanation for experience replay through improved mixing properties. The contribution is a finite-data account that explicitly connects temporal dependence, update choices, and learning progress.
neurips-2017-finite-sample-analysis-of-t.tldr: The paper gives finite-sample guarantees for GTD policy evaluation with Markov data, showing how step size and mixing time govern convergence.

paragraphs: Hypothesis transfer learning incorporates a model trained on a source domain into learning on a target domain. The paper develops a unified framework for analyzing this process while retaining dependence on the learning algorithm. Its central device is a transformation function that describes the relationship between the source and target domains.

The analysis focuses on excess risk, the gap between a learned predictor's risk and the relevant optimum. For kernel smoothing and kernel ridge regression, the authors show faster convergence of excess risk than in classical learning without transfer when the two domains are related. The relationship between domains is therefore a condition supporting the benefit, rather than transfer being universally advantageous.

The framework also includes an analysis of cross-validation for choosing a transfer technique. This selection procedure can return to ordinary learning when transfer is unhelpful. Experiments with robotics and neural imaging data demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. Together, the results connect potential gains from an existing model with a principled mechanism for deciding whether that model actually helps the target task.
neurips-2017-hypothesis-transfer-learnin.tldr: Transformation functions provide a framework for analyzing when a source model accelerates target learning and selecting when to use transfer.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering random variables into groups that are mutually independent. The desired answer is the finest such partition: separate the variables as much as possible while preserving independence between the resulting groups. The objects being clustered are variables, and the criterion concerns their joint distribution rather than ordinary geometric similarity.

Mutual independence makes this different from clustering based on pairwise measurements. A matrix of pairwise similarities does not capture the joint requirement the method must satisfy, so traditional clustering algorithms are inapplicable to the stated formulation. The distribution is generally unknown, and the method must infer its relevant structure from available observations.

The authors consider both independent sampling and stationary time series, emphasizing the more general time-series setting. They propose a computationally tractable, consistent algorithm for each case. Consistency gives an asymptotic correctness property as observations accumulate, while tractability addresses whether the procedure can be computed. The contribution establishes algorithms for a clustering objective whose defining statistical structure cannot be reduced to the usual pairwise matrix.
neurips-2017-independence-clustering-wit.tldr: The paper develops consistent, tractable methods for partitioning random variables into mutually independent groups without relying on pairwise similarity matrices.

paragraphs: A signal representation should ideally tolerate meaningful transformations while preserving the information needed to describe the signal. This paper examines deep representations that combine near-invariance to groups of transformations with stability under diffeomorphisms, or smooth invertible deformations. Near-invariance concerns limited sensitivity to transformations; stability concerns controlled changes when the signal is deformed.

The authors generalize a multilayer kernel introduced for convolutional kernel networks. They then study the geometry of its associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space, a mathematical space of functions defined by that kernel. This provides a framework for investigating transformation behavior together with preservation of signal information, rather than treating these as unrelated properties.

The paper establishes stability of the signal representation itself. It also shows that models belonging to the associated function space, including a large class of convolutional neural networks, may share that stability. The wording matters: the result identifies a route by which such models can inherit the property, rather than declaring that every convolutional network is automatically stable.
neurips-2017-invariance-and-stability-of.tldr: A generalized multilayer kernel explains how deep representations can preserve information while remaining near-invariant to transformations and stable under smooth deformations.

paragraphs: Koopman spectral analysis offers a way to study nonlinear dynamical systems through functions of their states. Dynamic mode decomposition is a numerical tool for this analysis, but it often requires manually chosen nonlinear observables. Choosing those functions can be difficult when the underlying dynamics are not known in advance.

The paper proposes learning the observables directly from data, guided by the idea of a Koopman invariant subspace. It seeks functions that transform observations into a representation where linear regression fits the dynamics well. The optimization criterion is the residual sum of squares from linear least-squares regression, so the quality of the linear fit directly guides representation learning.

The authors implement this approach with neural networks and evaluate it empirically on nonlinear dynamical systems and applications. Its central contribution is a data-driven alternative to manually preparing observables. The reported evaluation examines the learned representation in use; the abstract does not claim that the optimization always discovers an exactly invariant subspace for arbitrary dynamics.
neurips-2017-learning-koopman-invariant-.tldr: The method learns nonlinear observables from data by seeking a representation whose dynamics admit a good linear least-squares fit.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether players using exponential-weights learning converge to equilibrium in potential games. It focuses on limited feedback: players may have noisy information about all their strategies, or may observe only the payoff of the strategy they actually chose. These two information settings lead to different convergence statements.

In the semi-bandit setting, players receive noisy estimates of their payoff vectors, including unplayed strategies. The authors prove that play converges to a Nash equilibrium with probability one at a quasi-exponential rate. This establishes convergence of the sequence of play itself, beyond describing the method simply as a no-regret learning rule.

With bandit feedback, a constant exploration factor keeps every action's probability from becoming arbitrarily small. Under that modification, the corresponding result concerns approximate Nash equilibria. When exploration instead decreases suitably over time, play converges to an actual Nash equilibrium with probability one. These findings show how the amount of feedback and the exploration schedule shape the equilibrium guarantee available to the players.
neurips-2017-learning-with-bandit-feedba.tldr: Exponential-weights learning converges to equilibria in potential games under limited feedback, with the guarantee depending on exploration and available payoff information.

paragraphs: High-dimensional sparse learning seeks models that use relatively few variables, even when many are available. Nonconvex regularization can make the resulting optimization difficult. This paper proposes an algorithm that combines proximal Newton updates with a sequence of convex relaxations based on difference-of-convex programming.

The analysis uses structural properties of sparse models, specifically local restricted strong convexity and smoothness of the Hessian. Under these conditions, the authors prove local quadratic convergence within each convex-relaxation stage. Quadratic convergence describes very rapid error reduction near the relevant solution; the local qualification means the statement does not assert that every starting point immediately enjoys that behavior.

After only a few convex relaxations, the algorithm obtains a sparse approximate local optimum with optimal statistical properties under the analysis. This links computational progress with the quality of the estimated model, rather than treating optimization speed as the only objective. Numerical experiments support the theory. The stated endpoint remains an approximate local optimum, with the stronger statistical conclusion grounded in the sparse-model conditions.
neurips-2017-on-quadratic-convergence-of.tldr: A staged proximal Newton method achieves local quadratic convergence and strong statistical guarantees for nonconvex sparse learning under stated structural conditions.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves output spaces that can contain exponentially many classes. Learning often optimizes a convex surrogate loss in place of the actual task loss. This paper studies how reliably improvements in that surrogate translate into better task performance, while accounting for the size of the output space.

For any task loss, the authors construct a convex surrogate that can be optimized with stochastic gradient descent. They prove tight bounds on its calibration function, which relates excess surrogate risk to actual risk. This connection supplies consistency guarantees and quantifies how accurately the surrogate objective must be optimized to obtain useful performance on the task.

The analysis tracks the effect of exponentially many classes on both learning guarantees and optimization complexity. As a consequence, it formalizes why different task losses can make structured learning more or less difficult. In particular, the results identify the classical zero-one loss as ill-suited to structured prediction. The contribution therefore connects the choice of evaluation loss with both statistical requirements and computational demands.
neurips-2017-on-structured-prediction-th.tldr: The paper connects convex surrogate optimization to structured task risk through tight calibration bounds that account for exponentially large output spaces.

paragraphs: Online prediction with expert advice usually treats experts' reports as information a learner can combine. This paper studies binary prediction when experts act strategically to increase their own credibility. Their incentives become part of the learning problem, so a prediction algorithm must be analyzed together with the behavior it encourages.

The authors introduce a formal model and connect incentive-compatible algorithms to proper scoring rules. They also construct incentive-compatible algorithms with performance guarantees for absolute loss. This provides a positive result: it is possible to design prediction procedures that account for strategic reporting and still obtain meaningful guarantees.

The paper also proves lower bounds separating selfish experts from honest ones. Under the selfish-expert model and absolute loss, no online prediction algorithm, including randomized algorithms and algorithms that are not incentive compatible, achieves asymptotically vanishing regret. Thus, the obstruction is broader than a particular incentive design. The positive guarantees must be understood alongside this fundamental limit on what strategic expert advice permits.
neurips-2017-online-prediction-with-self.tldr: Strategic experts permit incentive-compatible prediction guarantees but impose a lower bound ruling out asymptotically vanishing regret under absolute loss.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning in two-player zero-sum stochastic games with an average-reward objective. Both the learner and an adversary influence immediate payoffs and state transitions. Learning therefore requires handling an opponent's behavior as well as uncertainty about the environment.

The proposed UCSG algorithm achieves sublinear regret relative to the game's value against an arbitrary opponent, improving previous results in the same setting. Sublinear regret means that the accumulated shortfall grows more slowly than the interaction horizon. The bound depends on the game's diameter, a quantity related to its mixing behavior, so the guarantee reflects how the dynamics allow movement through the game.

An extension finds a stationary policy that is within an error tolerance of the maximin objective, with sample complexity polynomial in the inverse tolerance up to logarithmic factors. The analysis develops perturbation bounds for Markov-chain mean first passage times and techniques for handling nonstationary opponents. These tools support guarantees in a setting where the adversary need not maintain a fixed behavior throughout learning.
neurips-2017-online-reinforcement-learni.tldr: UCSG achieves sublinear regret in average-reward stochastic games against arbitrary opponents and can be extended to learn approximately maximin stationary policies.

paragraphs: The paper develops a posterior-sampling reinforcement learning algorithm for communicating Markov decision processes with a finite but unknown diameter. Its objective is to control regret: the reward shortfall relative to an optimal infinite-horizon policy for undiscounted average reward, measured over a finite interaction horizon.

For S states, A actions, diameter D, and horizon T, the main result is a high-probability upper bound of order D√(SAT), suppressing logarithmic factors, when T is at least S⁵A. This improves the previously known upper bound of order DS√(AT). The improvement reduces the dependence on the number of states, an important distinction when comparing the guarantees as the state space grows.

The bound matches the state-count dependence of the established lower bound √(DSAT), while retaining a different dependence on diameter. The near-optimality claim therefore should not be read as exact agreement in every parameter. The proof also introduces anti-concentration results for Dirichlet distributions, providing mathematical tools that the authors suggest may be useful beyond this reinforcement learning analysis.
neurips-2017-optimistic-posterior-sampli.tldr: Optimistic posterior sampling improves worst-case regret's dependence on state count for communicating MDPs under a stated horizon condition.

paragraphs: Batch normalization changes how neural-network weights relate to the computation performed by a layer. This paper focuses on the invariance to linear scaling of weights and interprets the corresponding weight space as a Riemannian manifold. That geometric view makes the scaling symmetry central to the design of the learning algorithm.

The authors derive a learning rule that follows the manifold's intrinsic geometry. They describe the resulting rule as more efficient and easier to analyze. The same geometry also guides proposed gradient clipping and regularization methods, connecting these training choices to the structure of the normalized weight space.

Experiments across multiple network architectures and datasets show that the resulting algorithm consistently outperforms original batch normalization in the evaluated settings. The contribution is therefore both conceptual and algorithmic: a geometric interpretation produces concrete changes to optimization and its supporting procedures. The reported empirical result supports those changes across the tested cases, without implying that every possible architecture or dataset must show the same advantage.
neurips-2017-riemannian-approach-to-batc.tldr: A geometric treatment of batch-normalized weights yields a new learning rule, clipping method, and regularization approach with reported empirical gains.

paragraphs: Actor-critic reinforcement learning trains both an action-selecting policy and a component that evaluates behavior. This paper proposes ACKTR, which applies trust-region optimization to both components using Kronecker-factored approximate curvature, or K-FAC. The method extends the natural policy gradient framework with an approximation intended to make curvature-aware updates scalable.

Curvature information describes how the optimization landscape changes around the current parameters. ACKTR combines an approximation to that information with a trust region that controls the update. Applying the construction to both actor and critic gives the two parts of learning a shared optimization approach. The method handles continuous control and discrete policies learned directly from raw pixels.

The authors evaluate ACKTR on Atari games and MuJoCo control tasks. Against previous state-of-the-art on-policy actor-critic methods, they report higher rewards and an average two- to threefold improvement in sample efficiency. That average summarizes the evaluated comparisons; it is not a promise for every task. The findings support approximate curvature as a practical route to more efficient use of experience.
neurips-2017-scalable-trust-region-metho.tldr: ACKTR uses approximate curvature and trust regions for both actor and critic, reporting higher rewards and improved average sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can learn useful representations from high-dimensional inputs, while batch methods with linear representations offer stability and require less hyperparameter tuning. This paper combines those strengths in Least Squares Deep Q-Network, or LS-DQN. The goal is to retain learned features while using a linear least-squares method for part of the update.

The method periodically retrains the network's last hidden layer using a batch least-squares update. A Bayesian regularization term prevents this update from overfitting to more recent data. This makes the shallow retraining step part of a hybrid learning procedure, with deep representation learning and batch estimation contributing different capabilities.

Experiments on five Atari games show significant improvements over vanilla DQN and Double-DQN. The authors also investigate why the method improves performance and attribute the gain to the large batch size used when optimizing the last layer. That finding is central to interpreting the result: the evidence highlights how much data informs the shallow update, alongside the proposed least-squares formulation.
neurips-2017-shallow-updates-for-deep-re.tldr: LS-DQN combines deep features with regularized least-squares updates, with reported gains attributed to large batches for last-layer optimization.

paragraphs: The paper considers recovering an unknown vector from measurements that square the magnitude of its inner product with known vectors. Solving such quadratic systems is NP-hard in general. The authors develop a procedure with strong guarantees for certain random measurement models, using randomness in the problem structure to support efficient recovery.

The algorithm begins with weighted maximal-correlation initialization, computed using a few power iterations. It then refines the estimate through iteratively reweighted gradient-type updates. The weighting and reweighting regularization distinguish the method from prior approaches. Under the stated random models, it recovers the solution with high probability in time proportional to reading the data when the equation count is at least a constant times the number of unknowns.

The empirical findings include perfect high-dimensional recovery at the information-theoretic equation count and near-optimal statistical accuracy with additive noise. Tests using synthetic data and real images support improved recovery and computational efficiency relative to existing methods. The theoretical recovery guarantee and these empirical observations have different scopes: the guarantee explicitly depends on the random measurement model and sample requirement.
neurips-2017-solving-most-systems-of-ran.tldr: Weighted initialization and reweighted gradient updates enable efficient recovery for certain random quadratic systems, with strong empirical noise and sample-efficiency results.

paragraphs: The paper studies selecting at most k items to maximize a monotone submodular objective, which captures increasing value with diminishing returns. It adds two practical complications: items arrive as a stream, and m stored items may be removed after processing finishes. A useful summary must therefore remain valuable despite those later deletions.

The proposed STAR-T algorithm processes the data once and stores a short, robust summary. Its construction combines a partitioning structure with exponentially decreasing acceptance thresholds. After any m summary elements are removed, a simple greedy procedure called STAR-T-GREEDY operates on the remaining items and achieves a constant-factor approximation guarantee.

The guarantee directly addresses the uncertainty about which stored items will disappear. The streaming stage prepares a summary that supports selection after deletion, without needing the removed subset in advance. In two data summarization tasks, the method matches or outperforms existing greedy and streaming approaches, even when those comparison methods know the deleted subset beforehand. These experiments complement the theoretical robustness guarantee with evidence on the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2017-streaming-robust-submodular.tldr: STAR-T builds a one-pass summary that supports constant-factor submodular selection even after any specified number of stored items are deleted.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution by selecting a tractable distribution from a chosen family. The divergence commonly used for this selection can underestimate posterior variance, making the approximation appear too certain. This paper proposes CHIVI, a black-box inference algorithm that changes the divergence used to fit the approximation.

CHIVI minimizes a chi-divergence directed from the posterior toward the approximating distribution. It does so by minimizing an upper bound on model evidence, called CUBO. The authors report improved posterior uncertainty from this objective. Combined with the usual evidence lower bound, the upper bound also supplies a sandwich estimate that brackets the model evidence.

The evaluation covers probit regression, Gaussian process classification, and a Cox process model of basketball plays. Compared with expectation propagation and classical variational inference, CHIVI produces better error rates and more accurate posterior variance estimates in the reported studies. The results make uncertainty estimation a central criterion for evaluating the approximation, alongside prediction error and the ability to bound evidence.
neurips-2017-variational-inference-via-c.tldr: CHIVI minimizes a chi-divergence upper bound to improve posterior uncertainty estimates and complement the usual lower bound on model evidence.

paragraphs: The paper augments generative models with external memory by treating a memory read as a probabilistic operation. A read samples a discrete address and retrieves its contents, making the memory output a conditional mixture distribution. This interpretation gives memory addressing a place inside the model's probabilistic description.

Treating the address as a latent variable allows variational inference to train the memory module, using target information to guide lookups. Stochastic addressing also encourages multiple modes, matching an important feature of high-dimensional data. The formulation lets the authors quantify information gained through a lookup and measure how much the memory contributes to generation.

The authors incorporate the approach into a variational autoencoder for generative few-shot learning. The architectural intuition is that memory supplies a relevant template while the continuous part of the model represents remaining variations. Experiments show that the model can find relevant contents even when memory contains hundreds of unseen Omniglot characters. This supports the proposed division between selecting stored content and modeling variation around it.
neurips-2017-variational-memory-addressi.tldr: Modeling memory addresses as latent variables enables variational training of generative memory lookups and successful retrieval among unseen Omniglot characters.
